The landfill of plant byproducts is assumed to be outside the scope of the plants considered in this study; therefore, landfill leachate is not evaluated in this report. Intermittent discharges (e.g., chemical metal cleaning wastewater), coal pile runoff, low volume waste (e.g., boiler blowdown), and cooling tower blowdown were assumed to be compliant with all applicable regulations with no additional treatment beyond conventional considerations. Under the assumptions established in this section, no additional control technology considerations are required for the ammonia case studies to comply with the ELG rule. 2.7.3 CO Capture & Storage 2 Global CO emissions from the production of high-purity ammonia account for 500 MM tonnes 2 of CO annually. This is roughly equivalent to 1.8 percent of global CO emissions (The Royal 2 2 Society, 2020). However, the absence of environmental regulations targeting CO emissions 2 from industrial sources such as ammonia production plants limits the overall carbon capture efficiency at such facilities as well as industry-wide adoption of CO capture. 2 As led by the growing number of such projects, an objective of this study was to examine plant arrangements capable of achieving high carbon capture efficiencies. A study definition of “maximum CO capture” was established that considers the following: 2 24 COMPARISON OF COMMERCIAL, STATE-OF-THE-ART, FOSSIL-BASED AMMONIA PRODUCTION • A 2 x 3 water gas shift reactor arrangement was incorporated into each plant to increase the CO conversion efficiency to 97.2 percent. The conversion rate matches that of the E- GasTM (CB&I gasifier technology) integrated gasification combined cycle cases studied in the NETL Fossil Energy Baseline study, which employed the same reactor arrangement (Turner, et al., 2025) • The plant incorporates CO capture technologies that can capture 99 percent of the CO 2 2 in a pressurized syngas stream as well as capture 97 percent of the CO in low-pressure 2 flue gas • No partial bypasses of the AGR technologies are included as control mechanisms for targeting specific levels of CO capture in the plant flowsheets 2 • No adjustments have been made to vendor-provided CO separation efficiencies of the 2 AGR technologies The cost of CO T&S into a geologic formation is estimated using the Office of Fossil Energy 2 (FE)/NETL CO Transport Cost Model and the FE/NETL CO Saline Storage Cost Model (NETL, 2 2 2017a) (NETL, 2023). CO T&S were developed specifically for Case 2 (SMR w/ CCS) and Case 3 2 (ATR w/ CCS) in this study based on the CO product flow rate. Assumptions for CO T&S costs 2 2 include a 62-mile pipeline distance and storage in the Mount Simon reservoir located in the Illinois Basin.
